instruction: none: started by the service for timer
headline: This was a timer run with no instruction. It took up the line's three open items: the overlap that stopped the f* 0.3 seed 1 layer, the same-instant loop that stopped the f* 0.4 layer, and the cost of the contact-force solve. The overlap came from two spheres in one moving stack with no contact between them, which nothing checked. That pair is now watched (it acted once, and the overlap is gone), but the layer then stops in a same-instant loop. Both loops have one cause: a sphere joins, its new contact is found pulling and dropped, and it goes back still closing at round-off speed, so the same touch is found again. The force solve is now 6 to 10 times cheaper with the same results.

experiments.question: Where does the 'rider and free sphere overlap' that stopped the seed 1, f* 0.3 layer in the step to 5.93 come from?
experiments.what_was_done: The layer was saved at 5.92 and the next step was run with every stack handler logged, including the gaps of every sphere a handler hands back.
experiments.result: Two spheres, 84 and 93, belonged to the same five-sphere moving stack but had no contact with each other. The stack's integration never checks such pairs. When another sphere hit the stack hard enough to break it, the two came back as a free sphere and a riding sphere already overlapping by 4.6e-5 diameters and still closing. The engine then refused the overlap.
experiments.takeaway: The stack integration watched the plate and the side walls but not its own spheres. The fix (D0100) watches them the same way.

experiments.question: With pairs inside a stack watched, does seed 1 at f* 0.3 get past 5.93?
experiments.what_was_done: Seed 1 and seed 2 at f* 0.3 were rerun from the start with the new check (900 s CPU cap), plus a one-step run from the saved state.
experiments.result: In seed 1 the check acted once: the two spheres met slowly and were given a contact. The overlap did not recur, but the layer stopped in the same step on a loop at one instant, at 5.9205. Seed 2 ran exactly as before and reached 6.59 at the CPU cap; the check never acted there. The one-step run from the saved state was not a valid test, because that state was saved by the old code and already held the overlap.
experiments.takeaway: The fix works where it was aimed, but seed 1 still does not get through the step, so the experiment is falsified on its main clause.

experiments.question: What is the new loop in seed 1 at 5.9205?
experiments.what_was_done: The layer was saved at 5.92 with the new code and the step was traced.
experiments.result: In 36 of the 41 handler calls at that instant the same thing happens. Free sphere 86 touches sphere 84 of a moving stack at an approach speed of about one part in a billion billion (round-off). It joins, and at the new stack's start its contact is found pulling, so the contact is dropped. The sphere goes back free, still closing at round-off speed and 4e-14 diameters away, and the search finds the same touch again. Each repeat increases both the count of joins and the count of dropped contacts.
experiments.takeaway: The drop rule and the touch search disagree: the drop rule says the pair separates, but the search counts the leftover round-off approach as a new touch. The counts of joins and drops in this and earlier runs are inflated by these repeats.

experiments.question: What is the same-instant loop that stopped the f* 0.4 layer at 5.2816?
experiments.what_was_done: The layer was run to 5.28 with the code the loop was found with, saved, and the next step traced.
experiments.result: The loop recurs at the same instant. It starts when the contact between spheres 54 and 59 opens and their stack splits. Sphere 59 then touches 54 again at an approach speed of about 1e-16, joins, has its contact dropped as pulling, and goes back still closing. This happens in 40 of the 41 calls at that instant.
experiments.takeaway: It is the same mechanism as the seed 1 loop, so one fix should address both. As the checker said, most of the 43 'pull rule actions' reported for this layer last run were repeats of this loop.

experiments.question: Can the contact-force solve be made cheaper without changing its result?
experiments.what_was_done: The force matrix is now filled directly from each force's effect on the accelerations, instead of by evaluating the conditions once per unknown. On 300 random stacks, and on the offline replay of the original stall pair, the new and old builds were compared with the same inputs in one process.
experiments.result: Wherever the matrix is well conditioned (262 of 300 stacks), the two agree to two parts in a thousand million million. Each solve is six to ten times cheaper for stacks of two to five spheres, and the replay's stack part took 2.2 instead of 6.7 seconds. The other 38 random stacks have singular force matrices. Numpy's solver does not flag them, so the least-squares fallback added for that case never runs.
experiments.takeaway: This is a performance change with the same results. It has not yet been timed in a layer. Singular force matrices need a better check.

questions.question: Should a hit between the rest speed (0.01) and the wake speed (0.05) on a sphere in a moving stack bounce off it as if it could not move (as the design says for still spheres), or break the stack as now?
questions.why_it_matters: Most breaking hits in the test layers fall in this range. Breaking costs a rebuild each time and changes how long stacks last.
questions.default_if_unanswered: Keep breaking the stack (the current rule) until the layers run through a cycle, then measure both.

proposed_directions.direction: Fix the undone-join loop: when a joining contact is dropped as pulling, treat the pair's leftover round-off approach as no touch (check first why the existing round-off rule in the search does not catch it), and count only joins that hold. Test from the two saved states before the loops.
proposed_directions.rationale: It stops all three test layers that are not at the CPU cap, and saved states make each test take minutes instead of half an hour.

proposed_directions.direction: Detect singular contact-force matrices by their condition number and use the minimum-norm forces there; count how often real stacks hit them.
proposed_directions.rationale: Numpy does not flag them, so a stack with such a matrix gets forces dominated by round-off without anything noticing.

proposed_directions.direction: Time the cheaper force solve in the f* 0.4 layer, then locate contact changes from the integrator's dense output and join spheres that touch at one instant in one step.
proposed_directions.rationale: These are the remaining cost items from the last run's trace and the checker's review.
